title: Switzerland Launches Consultation on Stricter Bonus Rules for Banks
excerpt: The Swiss government has opened a public consultation on tougher banking regulations, including mandatory bonus deferrals for top executives, as part of its post-Credit Suisse overhaul.
body:
• Switzerland has launched a public consultation on stricter bonus rules for banks, requiring multi-year deferrals of variable compensation for top executives.
  • Under the proposals, bonuses can be clawed back for misconduct and banks must clearly assign responsibility for key decisions to senior managers.
  • Market regulator FINMA would gain new powers to levy fines and intervene earlier when risks emerge.
  • The measures are part of Switzerland's broader "too-big-to-fail" overhaul prompted by the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse.

Switzerland on Wednesday launched a public consultation on tougher banking regulations that would impose stricter rules on bonuses at UBS and other systemically important lenders, the latest step in the country's overhaul of its financial oversight framework following the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse.

Under the draft proposals, banks would be required to structure bonus schemes that reward long-term, sustainable performance and discourage excessive risk-taking, the Swiss government said. The rules carry particular weight for UBS, Switzerland's only remaining global bank following its government-brokered takeover of Credit Suisse in March 2023.

"The rules are designed to promote the positive development of an institution over the long term, and to counteract unfavourable risk behaviour."

— Swiss Federal Council statement

What the Proposals Require

A significant portion of variable compensation for top executives and high earners must be deferred for several years under the new framework. The government noted that internationally, deferral periods typically run four to five years.

If misconduct or losses emerge during the deferral period, banks will be required to reduce or cancel outstanding bonuses. In cases of proven wrongdoing, bonuses that have already been paid out could also be clawed back — a provision aimed at holding senior bankers personally accountable for risk decisions.

Banks with at least 250 employees would also be required to clearly assign responsibility for key decisions to senior managers, establishing a direct accountability chain.

Expanded Powers for FINMA

The consultation also addresses the powers of FINMA, Switzerland's financial markets regulator. Under the proposals, FINMA would gain the authority to impose fines on institutions and levy penalties for delays in implementing supervisory orders. It would also be able to intervene earlier when emerging risks are identified.

These changes address longstanding criticism that FINMA lacked the enforcement tools available to regulators in other major financial centers. During the Credit Suisse crisis, the regulator's limited powers came under scrutiny as the bank's rapid deterioration exposed gaps in Switzerland's oversight framework.

The Path to This Point

The consultation follows a turbulent period in Swiss banking regulation. The Swiss government first sketched out these rules last year as part of a broad package of 22 measures and more than 200 pages of recommendations on policing banks deemed "too big to fail."

Swiss lawmakers have been actively debating related proposals aimed at making UBS hold more capital — a contentious issue given that UBS's balance sheet, at roughly $1.7 trillion, now exceeds twice Switzerland's annual economic output.

In March 2026, the Council of States rejected an outright ban on bonuses at systemically important banks, which Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter called "quite radical." Instead, parliament has pushed for a regulatory approach that ensures compensation systems do not create perverse incentives. In a separate move last year, the lower house's economic committee removed a contentious plan to cap banker pay at 5 million Swiss francs.

What's Next

The public consultation period will allow industry stakeholders, financial institutions, and the public to comment on the draft proposals before they are finalized. Lawmakers are simultaneously debating the broader capital requirements package, which could require UBS to retain significantly more equity to back its foreign operations.

The reforms carry implications beyond Switzerland's borders. As the country that hosts major international banking operations and the Bank for International Settlements, its regulatory approach is closely watched by other jurisdictions grappling with similar questions about executive compensation and financial stability.
